justice: Spatial resources are unevenly distributed: a very wide vehicle carriageway occupies most of the corridor, while only one clearly visible sidewalk appears on the left side.
The right side is dominated by a green verge and parked trucks, but no visible pedestrian path is provided there, limiting equal access for all road users.
Accessibility is only moderate because the left sidewalk looks wide and relatively flat, yet no curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossing facilities are visible in the image.
Fairness is weakened by the roadside occupation of space by multiple parked freight trucks and a three-wheeler, which prioritizes motorized and freight use over walking and cycling.
safety: A posted 15 speed-limit sign suggests some speed control, which can improve safety in this industrial-looking street.
However, many large trucks are parked along both sides of the roadway, creating visibility obstruction and potential dooring or pull-out conflicts.
There is no visible protected bike lane, edge buffer, or pedestrian crossing, increasing exposure for non-motorized users.
Streetlights are present along the corridor, which supports nighttime safety, but the long straight road geometry may still encourage speeding when trucks are absent.
livability: The street appears dominated by logistics or industrial functions, with few active frontages, shops, or public destinations visible at street level.
Only one pedestrian is visible, indicating limited social activity and weak street vitality.
There are no visible benches, bus shelters, plazas, or community amenities that would support lingering or everyday social use.
The tree-lined green area on the right adds environmental quality, but it does not compensate for the overall low level of public-facing activity.
sustainability: A substantial row of mature trees and a grassy verge on the right contribute to carbon capture, shade, and local ecological value.
The corridor lacks visible dedicated cycling infrastructure, which weakens support for low-carbon transport.
The street design still heavily prioritizes trucks and private motor vehicles through a wide asphalt carriageway.
No visible permeable paving, bioswale, rain garden, or other stormwater management feature can be identified from the image.
aesthetics: The continuous line of mature trees on the right creates a pleasant green edge and improves the visual character of the street.
The sky is open and the roadway is relatively clean, which gives the scene a spacious and orderly appearance.
Aesthetics are reduced by the long line of parked freight trucks and the utilitarian industrial building on the left.
Overhead utility wires and the very wide expanse of asphalt make the corridor feel functional rather than visually refined.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: the trees on the right provide shade, but the main roadway and left-side sidewalk are largely exposed to direct sun.
Physical comfort for pedestrians is limited because no seating, resting points, or protective buffers from traffic are visible.
The left sidewalk appears wide and smooth, which supports basic walking comfort where it exists.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the presence of many large trucks, the broad traffic space, and the sparse pedestrian activity, which can make the environment feel inhospitable.
walkability: Walkability is constrained because a clear sidewalk is visible only on the left side, while the right side lacks an obvious pedestrian path.
There is no marked crosswalk, pedestrian refuge, or curb ramp visible, reducing connectivity across the street.
The left sidewalk seems wide and relatively even, which is a positive feature for straightforward walking movement.
Long blocks, low frontage activity, and truck-dominated roadside conditions make walking less attractive for everyday trips.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, protected cycle track, or shared-lane marking is visible anywhere on the corridor.
Cyclists would have to share space with large trucks and parked freight vehicles, creating high perceived and actual conflict risk.
The wide carriageway may provide some lateral space in practice, but without markings or protection it remains uncomfortable for most riders.
No bicycle parking, bike signals, or intersection treatments for cyclists are visible in the scene.
